summary: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDC) is a CNAPP that fuses CSPM — continuous configuration assessment scored via a single Secure Score against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB) — with CWP, the per-resource Defender workload-protection plans that raise runtime threat alerts. It spans Azure, AWS, GCP, and Arc-connected on-premises resources. The free foundational CSPM tier ships by default with every Azure subscription; the paid Defender CSPM tier adds attack-path analysis, the cloud security explorer graph, agentless scanning, DevOps posture, and EASM insights. A regulatory compliance dashboard separately maps the same environment against formal standards (ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, NIST SP 800-53, CIS, SOC 2) with pass/fail evidence per control.
keyPoints: **CNAPP = CSPM + CWP** in one product: CSPM continuously evaluates configuration against best practices and answers 'are we configured safely?'; CWP runs per-resource 'Defender for X' threat-protection plans and answers 'are we being attacked right now?'. Works across **Azure, AWS, GCP, and on-premises via Azure Arc**.

**Secure Score**: a single percentage aggregating how many impact-weighted recommendations have been satisfied. Recommendations are grouped into **security controls**, and a control only contributes its points once **every** resource inside it is healthy — remediate the highest-impact recommendations first to raise the score fastest.

**Free (Foundational CSPM)** — active by default on every Azure subscription: Secure Score, asset inventory, and MCSB-based recommendations. **Defender CSPM** (paid) adds **agentless scanning**, **attack-path analysis**, the **cloud security explorer** (security-graph queries), data-aware posture, code-to-cloud/DevOps posture, EASM insights, and governance rules.

**Attack path analysis** and the **cloud security explorer** are Defender CSPM features only — not part of the free tier. A scenario like 'show internet-exposed VMs with a known vulnerability that can reach a database holding sensitive data' is the signature attack-path/security-explorer question.

**Regulatory compliance dashboard**: MCSB applies by default; add other standards at **management group or subscription** scope via `Defender for Cloud ▸ Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies ▸ Security policies ▸ Add more standards`. Each control shows pass/fail with evidence — usable directly as audit preparation.

**Workload protection (CWP) plans**: per-resource-type Defender plans (Servers, Storage, SQL/Databases, Containers, Key Vault, App Service, Resource Manager, APIs, AI services), toggled independently under `Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ (subscription) ▸ Defender plans`. Enabling one plan never auto-enables another — each carries its own cost and alert set.

**Multicloud connectors**: AWS and GCP accounts are onboarded using each cloud's **native identity federation** — no long-lived keys stored in Azure. For AWS, a downloaded **CloudFormation template** creates the trusted IAM role MDC assumes; GCP uses an equivalent Cloud Shell/Terraform script. Connected resources then get Secure Score, recommendations, and Defender plans alongside Azure.

**Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management (MDVM)** looks **inward**: missing patches and vulnerable software (CVEs) on machines and container images, feeding Secure Score. **External Attack Surface Management (EASM)** looks **outward**: it crawls the internet to discover domains, IPs, certificates, and services the organization owns — including forgotten shadow IT — before an attacker finds them first.
commonPitfalls: Don't confuse **CSPM** (posture/configuration — free tier available) with **CWP** (runtime threat detection via paid Defender plans) — the free tier is CSPM only, it never includes workload-protection alerts.

**Attack path analysis** and the **cloud security explorer** are **Defender CSPM (paid)** features, not free-tier capabilities — any scenario requiring exploit-chain visualization or security-graph queries implies upgrading beyond foundational CSPM.
**MCSB is the default baseline**, not something you replace with ISO 27001/PCI-DSS/NIST — those are **added on top** of MCSB, at management group or subscription scope.

Don't swap **MDVM** (inward: CVEs/missing patches on owned machines and images) with **EASM** (outward: attacker's-eye discovery of internet-facing assets) — 'find CVEs on this VM' is MDVM; 'discover internet-facing assets we didn't know we owned' is EASM.
Multicloud connectors use **native federation**, never stored long-lived secrets — a proposed design that pastes a permanent AWS access key/secret into the Azure connector is wrong.
Enabling a Defender plan for one resource type (e.g., Servers) does **not** enable another (e.g., Storage or SQL) — each plan is an independent toggle and cost line.

commands.task: List the pricing tier (Free vs Standard) of every Defender plan on a subscription
Enable a specific Defender workload-protection plan, e.g. Defender for Storage
commands.cli: az security pricing create --name StorageAccounts --tier Standard

commands.cli: az graph query -q "Resources | where type == 'microsoft.storage/storageaccounts' | project name, location"
commands.powershell: Search-AzGraph -Query "Resources | where type == 'microsoft.storage/storageaccounts' | project name, location"

summary: Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native SIEM+SOAR, layered on top of a Log Analytics workspace: data connectors ingest logs from Microsoft cloud sources, on-premises servers, and network appliances; analysts query everything in KQL; analytics rules raise alerts that group into incidents; and automation rules plus Logic App playbooks drive the response. Access is governed by Azure RBAC plus Sentinel-specific Reader/Responder/Contributor roles. Since Sentinel's move into the unified Microsoft Defender portal, its incidents merge with Defender XDR's into a single investigation queue with cross-product advanced hunting.
keyPoints: **Sentinel = SIEM** (collect, store, correlate, alert on logs from many sources) **+ SOAR** (automate response via playbooks), built **on top of a Log Analytics workspace**, which is the storage and query boundary.

**Sentinel RBAC roles** layer on top of Azure RBAC: **Reader** (view data/incidents), **Responder** (Reader + manage incidents — assign, change status, comment), **Contributor** (Responder + create/edit analytics rules, workbooks, playbooks). A separate **Playbook Operator** role runs/attaches playbooks without granting full Contributor.

**Content hub** is Sentinel's marketplace of bundled **solutions** (data connectors + analytics rules + workbooks + hunting queries + playbooks) for a given product, e.g. 'Microsoft Entra ID' or 'AWS'.

**Data connector patterns**: Microsoft cloud sources (Entra ID, M365, Defender XDR, Azure activity) use **native, clicks-only connectors**; Windows Security events use the **Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) + a Data Collection Rule (DCR)** selecting the event set (All/Common/Minimal/Custom), or **Windows Event Forwarding (WEF)** to a collector; on-prem/firewall appliances use **CEF/Syslog via an AMA-based Linux forwarder**; fully custom sources use the **Logs Ingestion API/DCR** or the **Codeless Connector Platform**.

**Detection-to-response chain**: **analytics rules** (mostly scheduled KQL, plus Microsoft-security and ML rules) raise **alerts** → correlated alerts become an **incident** → **automation rules** apply lightweight if/then logic (set severity, assign owner, close noise, invoke a playbook) → a **playbook** (Azure Logic App) performs the actual external action (post to Teams/ServiceNow, disable a user, isolate a device).

**Automation rule ≠ playbook**: the automation rule is the trigger/condition layer over an incident that can invoke a playbook; the playbook is the Logic App that does the heavy external work. A **SOC optimization** recommendation only flags coverage gaps or costly low-value data — it is not itself a detection.

**Retention tiers**: **interactive/analytics retention** is fast to query (up to 2 years, first 90 days free) for active detection/hunting; cheaper **long-term/archive retention** (up to 12 years) suits compliance data that's rarely queried.

**Unified Microsoft Defender portal**: Sentinel now operates there, merging Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents into **one queue**, with **advanced hunting KQL spanning both**; Microsoft Purview Audit logs also surface there for unified investigation.

When no connector exists, data reaches Sentinel through a **custom log table**: create the table in the Log Analytics workspace (its name ends in `_CL`), define a **Data Collection Rule** with the schema and any transformation, and post to the **Logs Ingestion API** against the DCR endpoint. The **Codeless Connector Platform** reaches the same destination declaratively, for a source that exposes an API you can poll.

The **DCR transformation** is where cost and quality are decided before ingestion: a KQL transform can drop columns, filter rows and reshape fields on the way in, so you pay to store what you will query rather than everything the source emits. Getting the schema wrong is expensive to undo — a custom table's columns are far easier to define correctly once than to change later.
commonPitfalls: **Automation rule ≠ playbook**: don't describe the automation rule as performing the external action — it triggers/conditions and can invoke a playbook, which is the Logic App that actually acts.

Map the verb to the exact role: **view only** → Reader; **triage/assign/close incidents** → Responder; **create detections/automation** → Contributor. Running a playbook additionally needs **Playbook Operator** or permissions on the underlying Logic App.
Never propose the retired **Log Analytics agent (MMA)** for new telemetry collection — **AMA + DCR** is the only supported path for Windows Security events today.
'Keep logs 7 years for audit, rarely queried' = **long-term/archive retention**, not the interactive analytics tier, which is far more expensive for that use case.
**CEF/Syslog** ingestion needs an **AMA-based Linux forwarder/collector** — it is not a one-click native connector like Entra ID's.
A **SOC optimization** recommendation is advisory (coverage gap or cost/value tuning), not an alert or incident by itself.
Creating the custom table and expecting data to appear — nothing arrives until a **DCR exists and something posts to its ingestion endpoint**. The table is the destination, not the pipeline.
Ingesting the full payload into a custom table and planning to filter at query time: the ingestion charge is already incurred. Filtering belongs in the **DCR transformation**, before the data lands.

Create a Data Collection Rule from a JSON definition, for a custom log table fed by the Logs Ingestion API

summary: Microsoft Security Copilot is a generative-AI assistant for security teams that reasons over an organization's security data through plugins connecting to Defender, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, Purview, and third-party tools, answering natural-language prompts like 'summarize this incident' or 'explain this KQL query.' It runs standalone in its own dedicated portal or embedded as panels inside other Microsoft security portals, with capacity billed by provisioned Security Compute Units (SCU) and owner/contributor roles separating administration from day-to-day use. Promptbooks package repeatable multi-step investigations, while autonomous agents run entire tasks — like phishing triage — end-to-end without analyst prompting.
keyPoints: **SCU (Security Compute Unit)**: the provisioned, hourly-billed capacity that powers Copilot; scale SCUs up or down to manage cost and throughput.

**First-time setup**: provision SCU capacity in Azure (`Create a resource ▸ Microsoft Security Copilot ▸ capacity`), then on first portal launch set the **default environment** — geo, the Azure subscription/resource group backing the capacity, and where Copilot may store data.

**Roles**: **owner** manages settings, capacity, role assignments, and plugins; **contributor** uses Copilot and runs sessions. By default, **any Microsoft Entra user in the tenant** can be made contributor; only owners control plugin enablement and data-sharing.

**Plugins** decide what Copilot can see and do: Microsoft plugins (Defender XDR, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, Purview, Threat Intelligence), third-party plugins, and custom plugins built via API or KQL — enabled under `Settings ▸ Plugins`.
**Promptbooks** package a saved, reusable sequence of prompts that runs a multi-step task the same way every time (e.g., a standard incident-investigation workflow) — a human still triggers them.

**Agents** are autonomous Copilot workers (from Microsoft or the Security Store) that run a security task end-to-end without step-by-step prompting — e.g., a Phishing Triage agent that investigates and closes low-risk reports — freeing analysts from repetitive work.

**Standalone vs embedded**: standalone is the dedicated Copilot portal with a free-form prompt bar and promptbooks; embedded means Copilot panels appear directly inside other portals (Defender, Intune, Entra, Purview) without switching tools.
**RBAC-bounded answers**: Copilot's responses are governed by the querying user's existing permissions and the plugins enabled for the environment — it never bypasses RBAC, even for the owner role.
commonPitfalls: 'Summarize this incident from inside the Defender portal' = **embedded** mode; 'open Security Copilot and run an investigation promptbook' = **standalone** mode — don't swap the two.
If Copilot 'can't see' some data, check first whether the **relevant plugin is enabled** and whether the **user has rights** to that data — don't assume a model limitation.
**Owner vs contributor**: only owner manages plugins/capacity/role assignments; a request to 'let an analyst enable new plugins' needs **owner**, not contributor — contributor is usage-only.
**Promptbook ≠ agent**: a promptbook is a saved sequence a human still runs; an **agent** executes autonomously with zero step-by-step prompting.
SCU capacity is **provisioned ahead of time and billed hourly** like Azure compute — it is not a per-seat license, and under-provisioning throttles usage rather than blocking specific users.
Copilot **never bypasses RBAC** — granting the owner role does not let someone see data their existing permissions and enabled plugins don't already allow.
